title: 'Genital theft' accusations: How social media fuelled rumours that turned deadly
description: More than 80 people were killed  between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Glo
body: More than 80 people were killed  between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media."They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those  convinced he was a genital thief. His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008. They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience."If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob. Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire."After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals."Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence. The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online. "We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention"."Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw."It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said."To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

schema.headline: 'Genital theft' accusations: How social media fuelled rumours that turned deadly

title: Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village, officials say
description: Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who local officials say were killed by Israeli settlers and soldiers in an attack on their vil
body: Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who local officials say were killed by Israeli settlers and soldiers in an attack on their village in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.The village council in al-Mughayyir told the BBC that Omar al-Nassan, 19, and Khalil Abu Alia, 16, were killed as they tried to stop Israeli settlers stealing sheep and that confrontations broke out.The Israeli military stated that its forces had entered the village to provide security for an Israeli civilian and police trying to retrieve livestock.It said the forces fired on and struck what it called "key instigators" of a "violent disturbance", in which Palestinians threw stones at its troops.The deaths come amid a recent surge in settler violence in the West Bank, with more than three attacks per day on average recorded by the UN so far this year.Al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, has seen repeated settler attacks.WhatsApp messages in groups used by settlers have indicated that they hope to force its population to move.At least 81 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN's figures. At least 23 of those deaths have occurred in the context of settler attacks.Three Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, the UN says.The Israeli military has faced mounting criticism for actively participating in settler attacks on Palestinians, standing by, or failing to prosecute those responsible.On Thursday, Israel's police force said a 19-year-old settler had been arrested on suspicion of participating in an attack on the Palestinian village of Qusra on Saturday. It marks the first such arrest in weeks of attacks on Qusra.Dozens of masked settlers descended on the village, surrounding a house while Palestinians were trapped inside, and throwing stones.Israeli soldiers who were deployed to the scene reportedly detained the trapped Palestinians but not the settlers, allowing them to leave. The Israeli military said troops removed "rioters" and protected residents.Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.The settlements are illegal under international law.In a separate development on Wednesday, Israeli forces demolished the Palestinian village of Khirbet al-Tabban, in the Masafer Yatta area.Israeli human rights group B'Tselem said the village's 70 residents, including 28 children, were given no warning prior to the demolition and were not allowed to remove their property.It described the demolition as the most significant in Masafer Yatta since May 2025.In the 1980s, the Israeli military declared about 3,000 hectares in the South Hebron Hills, which includes Masafer Yatta, as a restricted firing zone for training purposes.The military says the Palestinian homes there have been built illegally.In 2022, Israel's Supreme Court ruled to allow the demolition of homes in the firing zone and the expulsion of their residents, who had argued that such a move violated international law and that their families had been living there since before the State of Israel was established.B'Tselem says Khirbet al-Tabban is the 66th Palestinian community to be expelled by Israeli authorities since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, which it alleges is part of a campaign of "ethnic cleansing" being carried out in the West Bank.

title: Embattled Spanish PM Sánchez insists no prior warnings before Ceuta crisis
description: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said no-one foresaw the influx of 72,000 migrants in the exclave of Ceuta, as pressure mounts over his handli
body: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said no-one foresaw the influx of 72,000 migrants in the exclave of Ceuta, as pressure mounts over his handling of the crisis."It's absurd to think that the government knew and did nothing," Sánchez told Spain's parliament on Thursday, hours after tens of thousands of people joined protests across the country backed by opposition parties.Sánchez also maintained there was no evidence Morocco was behind the mass crossing and there had been "close co-ordination" between the two countries.A Spanish police report has highlighted the "total permissiveness" of Moroccan security forces, although senior officials insist it does not point the finger at Rabat.Although most of the migrants have been sent back to Morocco, some 5,000 remain on the streets and beaches of Ceuta, on the North African coast, including as many as 1,400 children.There have been several reports that Spanish officials had been warned of a rise in sea arrivals over the border at Ceuta, following a Spanish court ruling that many migrants misunderstood to mean they would not be pushed back if they swam across.Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo accused the government of lying and a cover-up, and said the prime minister should resign.Spain's handling of the migrant influx angered some of its European partners, and Italy responded by imposing border restrictions on arrivals from Spain. The large turnout for the demonstrations in Madrid and other cities on Wednesday underlined the pressure Sánchez is under domestically too.The protests were ostensibly held to express support for the people of Ceuta, but as frequent anti-government chants have shown, they also reflected public anger at the ongoing crisis.Politicians to both his left and right point to what they say is Morocco's track record of using the border with Spain as leverage when it has a grievance. Many have interpreted the police report pointing to the role of Moroccan security forces in the July crossing as reinforcing this theory, although Sánchez maintained there was no solid evidence of government involvement.The report, commissioned by a High Court judge, said security forces had "made no serious attempt" to stop the influx and quoted some migrants saying Moroccan gendarmes had even provided guidance.Responding to the revelations, as well as media reports before the influx, Feijóo told MPs that the crisis had "originated in Morocco, was consented to by Morocco and there are indications that Morocco co-ordinated it and the government knew because it had been warned about it".Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.Sánchez said King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta and Melilla in the coming weeks to convey Spain's commitment to the two cities, although officials say no date has been set.He praised the response of Ceuta police who had chosen to "defend human life" when the influx took place, rather than defend the border. He also highlighted close co-operation with Moroccan authorities over the return of more than 90% of the migrants in the following 72 hours.He addressed the "difficult times" faced by the residents of Ceuta, as he explained the "complexity" of what had happened on 30 and 31 July.  He spoke of an "episode in which numerous actors and interests converge", doubling down on his assertion that hoaxes and rumours spread by social media had sparked the crisis.He has already blamed trafficking gangs and angered Russia and Israel for highlighting social media linked to both countries along with "an international far-right movement". He told MPs that there was no evidence of state actors being involved but doubled down on his allegations of accounts linked to the two countries.Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", he added.

title: Pig kidney works in human body for 271 days - is this the future of organ transplants?
description: A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.Tim Andrews said the transplant gave
body: A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list. Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis."I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel"."Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

title: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors unwind in Thailand by shopping and bar-hopping
description: Night, though, is when this resort city comes into its own, putting on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars. Pattaya's tourism industry
body: Night, though, is when this resort city comes into its own, putting on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars. Pattaya's tourism industry has been hit by conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.Local establishments have been hoping American sailors, arriving with nine months of unspent salary while at sea, will provide a much-needed boost. On Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to them, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier. They have, however, been reminded the sex industry is off-limits, as prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand. But alcohol was flowing. By midnight some of the younger sailors were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.
